idiom_name: function-local static std::unordered_map<Key, std::shared_ptr<T>> guarded by std::mutex
implementation_notes: Modern C++ composes the registry by hand from the standard library: a function-local static std::unordered_map (guaranteed to be initialised exactly once since C++11) holding std::shared_ptr instances, a std::mutex held across find-or-emplace, and try_emplace(...)->second to return the canonical instance. Returning shared_ptr makes the shared lifetime explicit and keeps entries alive while an insertion may rehash the map; std::call_once/once_flag fits when the whole table is built once at startup and lookups are read-only afterwards. Pre-C++11 the same shape needs pthreads and raw pointers, and the classic form is justified when the key set is algorithmic and no composition root can hand the instances around.
pitfalls: Function-local statics guarantee that the map is constructed once, not that find-or-insert is atomic: without the mutex two threads each build a Conn and one is dropped while its socket stays open.
Returning a raw pointer or reference into the map while another thread inserts into the same map is a data race on the container - return shared_ptr, or hold the lock across the whole access.
Static destruction order: the registry and the mutex are destroyed at exit, so an instance whose destructor calls conn_for() runs against a destroyed registry.
Pre-C++11 toolchains have no thread-safe magic statics, so the map needs an explicit pthread_once or once_flag guard as well as the lock.
